The Imperative to Erase: Why Columbus Day Must Fall as a Federal Holiday

The second Monday in October arrives annually, draped in the veneer of celebration—a federal holiday ostensibly commemorating "discovery" and "new beginnings." Yet, Columbus Day stands not as a tribute to exploration, but as a grotesque monument to genocide, colonial violence, and the systematic dehumanization that ushered in centuries of Indigenous suffering. To continue enshrining Christopher Columbus as a figure worthy of national honor is not merely historically ignorant; it is an active affirmation of the very ideologies of conquest, exploitation, and racial superiority that he personified. It is time, long overdue, to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday, acknowledging the horrific reality of his legacy and replacing it with a genuine commitment to truth, remembrance, and respect for the original peoples of this continent.

The core argument for abolition rests on the irrefutable, documented barbarity of Columbus's actions and their immediate, devastating consequences. Far from the benevolent navigator of myth, Columbus was a ruthless colonial administrator whose primary goals were extraction of wealth (gold, spices) and subjugation of Indigenous populations for Spain. Upon arriving in the Caribbean in 1492, he encountered the Taino people. His initial interactions quickly devolved into enslavement, torture that defies modern comprehension, and systematic terror. Historical records, including Columbus's own logs and the damning testimony of his contemporary, Bartolomé de las Casas, paint a harrowing picture:

  • Enslavement and Forced Labor: Columbus immediately took Indigenous people as slaves, sending thousands back to Spain in chains. He instituted the encomienda system, a thinly veiled form of forced labor where Indigenous communities were "granted" to Spanish colonists, who extracted brutal quotas of gold or crops. Failure meant amputation of hands or death.
  • Systematic Terror and Massacre: To enforce submission, Columbus employed public dismemberation, burning people alive, and unleashing ferocious dogs to tear apart those who resisted. Las Casas documented horrific acts: "They made bets as to who would slit a man open or cut off his head in a single stroke... or who would pierce a child's heart with his dagger."
  • Genocidal Demographic Collapse: The most profound testament to Columbus's legacy is the near-annihilation of the Indigenous populations he encountered. Within his first governorship (1494-1500), the Indigenous population of Hispaniola plummeted from an estimated 250,000 to 60,000 due to murder, forced labor, starvation, and, critically, the introduction of European diseases to which they had no immunity – a consequence accelerated by the horrific living conditions imposed by the colonial system. This was not accidental; it was the direct result of policies enacted under Columbus's command. While disease was a major factor later, the initial catastrophic collapse was driven by the violence and exploitation he initiated. Historians like David Stannard (American Holocaust) and Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz (An Indigenous Peoples' History of the United States) unequivocally identify the Columbian encounter as the genesis of a genocidal process that would engulf the entire hemisphere.

To celebrate this individual as a symbol of discovery fundamentally ignores the prior existence and sophisticated civilizations of the 50+ million Indigenous people already thriving across the Americas for millennia. It perpetuates the damaging and false narrative that the land was "empty" or its inhabitants "uncivilized savages" awaiting European salvation – a narrative that was crucial ideological justification for centuries of subsequent colonization, land theft, broken treaties, forced assimilation, and cultural erasure. Columbus Day doesn't honor exploration; it celebrates the theft of a world that was already found and inhabited. Honoring the initiator of this catastrophic chain of events, rather than the enduring resilience of the Indigenous nations he targeted, is a profound moral inversion.

Furthermore, the continued existence of Columbus Day as a federal holiday is a deep, ongoing wound and an official affront to Native American, First Nations, and Indigenous peoples across the continent. It sends a state-sanctioned message that their history of suffering at the hands of colonialism is irrelevant, that their ancestors' resistance is unimportant, and that the foundational violence of the United States and its hemisphere-wide legacy is something to be commemorated with a day off work. For Indigenous communities actively working to heal intergenerational trauma, revitalize languages and cultures suppressed for centuries, and fight for sovereignty and land rights, this holiday is a daily reminder of historical denial and contemporary marginalization. It is impossible to reconcile the federal government's stated commitments to tribal sovereignty and reconciliation with the act of formally celebrating the man whose voyages directly precipitated the destruction of countless Indigenous societies.

Proponents of Columbus Day often retreat to two defenses, both utterly insufficient. First, the "man of his time" argument rings hollow. Las Casas, a contemporary Spaniard and initially a colonist himself, recognized the horror at the time and became a fierce advocate, explicitly blaming Columbus and his system. Moral judgment is not anachronistic when the crimes involved are universally recognized as atrocities – enslavement, mass murder, torture. Second, the argument that it celebrates Italian-American heritage is misplaced. While Italian immigrants faced discrimination and sought positive symbols, honoring Columbus specifically is a poor and harmful vehicle for that pride. His actions have no positive bearing on Italian identity. Moreover, many Italian-Americans themselves, recognizing the truth, actively support replacing the holiday (as evidenced by organizations like the National Italian American Foundation shifting focus). Heritage should be celebrated through the actual contributions of Italian immigrants to American society – labor, culture, art – not through the veneration of a brutal colonizer whose connection to modern Italy is tenuous at best and whose legacy is universally toxic to others.

The solution is not to erase history, but to correct the historical record we choose to honor with a federal holiday. The growing movement to replace Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day provides the perfect, necessary alternative. This day, recognized by hundreds of cities, counties, and at least ten states, shifts the focus to celebrating the actual discoverers, the original inhabitants, and their enduring cultures, contributions, and resilience. It acknowledges the past with honesty while looking forward to building respectful, equitable relationships based on truth. Abolishing Columbus Day as a federal holiday would be a symbolic yet powerful step in the long-overdue process of national reconciliation. It declares that the United States no longer finds glory in conquest and genocide but instead seeks to honor the truth of its origins and the dignity of the peoples who have endured its darkest chapters.

Continuing to observe Columbus Day is an act of historical betrayal and moral negligence. It clings to a romanticized myth while ignoring the blood that stains Columbus's legacy. The federal government has a responsibility to ensure its official symbols reflect foundational American values – values of liberty, equality, and human dignity – which Columbus's actions so flagrantly violated. To persist in celebrating the architect of such profound suffering is not patriotism; it is complicity in the erasure of truth and the perpetuation of harm against Indigenous nations. We must summon the courage to confront our history accurately. We must dismantle the false idol on Columbus Day and replace it with a day that truly honors the first peoples of this land and the possibility of a more just future built on reconciliation, not denial. The time for abolition is not coming; it is long past due. Let the second Monday in October become a day not of misplaced celebration, but of genuine remembrance, respect, and the hard work of truth-telling that a nation committed to justice must undertake.

Replacing Columbus Day with a holiday honoring Indigenous Peoples (often called Indigenous Peoples' Day, Native American Day, or similar) is driven by a critical reevaluation of history, a commitment to truth-telling, and the pursuit of justice and healing. Here's a breakdown of the key reasons and supposed benefits, focusing on the harms of celebrating Columbus and the positive impact of recognizing Indigenous peoples:

I. The Harms of Celebrating Columbus Day: Why the Current Holiday is Problematic

  1. Glorifying a Symbol of Genocide, Enslavement, and Violence:

    • Historical Reality: Christopher Columbus's expeditions (1492 onwards) initiated the sustained European colonization of the Americas, which had catastrophic consequences for Indigenous populations. Columbus himself:
      • Enslaved Indigenous people: He shipped thousands of Taíno people from the Caribbean back to Europe as slaves. His own writings detail plans to capture and enslave Indigenous people, viewing them primarily as a source of labor and profit.
      • Instigated brutal violence: His governorship of Hispaniola involved horrific punishments (like cutting off hands for failing to meet gold quotas), massacres, and the systematic use of terror to subjugate Indigenous populations.
      • Initiated the transatlantic slave trade: After the Indigenous population was decimated (partly by his policies) and proved less compliant than expected, Columbus advocated for and facilitated the importation of enslaved Africans to replace them.
      • Caused catastrophic demographic collapse: While disease was a major factor later, the immediate violence, forced labor, famine due to disrupted societies, and despair caused by Columbus's regime led to the rapid and horrific decline of the Taíno population under his direct rule.
    • The Problem: Celebrating Columbus as a heroic "discoverer" erases this brutal reality. It venerates the initiator of a system that led directly to:
      • The deaths of tens of millions of Indigenous people (through violence, disease, and societal collapse).
      • Centuries of colonization, land theft, forced assimilation, cultural destruction, and systemic oppression that Indigenous nations continue to grapple with today.
      • The foundational injustice upon which the United States and many other Americas nations were built.

  2. Perpetuating Harmful Myths and Erasing Indigenous Presence:

    • The "Discovery" Myth: The celebration reinforces the false and Eurocentric notion that the Americas were "empty" or "unknown" lands before 1492. This ignores the fact that sophisticated, diverse Indigenous civilizations had thrived for thousands of years prior, with complex societies, cultures, technologies, and relationships with the land.
    • Erasing Indigenous History and Continuity: By focusing solely on Columbus as the starting point of American history, the holiday implicitly erases millennia of Indigenous history, culture, and sovereignty. It frames Indigenous peoples as passive victims of an inevitable "progress," rather than nations with rich, ongoing histories.
    • Perpetuating Stereotypes: The Columbus narrative often relies on and reinforces dehumanizing stereotypes of Indigenous peoples as "savages" who needed "civilizing," ignoring their diversity, resilience, and contributions.

  3. Inflicting Ongoing Pain on Indigenous Communities:

    • For Indigenous peoples, Columbus Day is a stark reminder of the trauma, loss, and ongoing injustices stemming from colonization. Celebrating the man who began centuries of genocide, land theft, and cultural suppression is profoundly hurtful and offensive. It signals that their history, suffering, and survival are not valued or acknowledged by the dominant society.

II. The Benefits of Recognizing Indigenous Peoples' Day: Positive Impacts

  1. Centers Truth and Historical Accuracy:

    • Correcting the Narrative: Indigenous Peoples' Day shifts the focus from a mythologized European "discoverer" to the actual inhabitants who had been here for millennia. It acknowledges the true starting point of American history – Indigenous civilizations.
    • Highlighting Continuity and Resilience: It recognizes that Indigenous peoples are not relics of the past but vibrant, ongoing nations with distinct cultures, languages, governance, and contributions that continue to shape the continent. It emphasizes survival and resilience against overwhelming attempts at erasure.

  2. Honors Indigenous Cultures, Contributions, and Sovereignty:

    • Celebrating Rich Diversity: The holiday provides a platform to celebrate the immense diversity of Indigenous cultures, languages, arts, knowledge systems (like sustainable agriculture and environmental stewardship), and spiritual traditions across hundreds of distinct nations.
    • Acknowledging Contributions: It brings recognition to the vast contributions Indigenous peoples have made (and continue to make) to the world – from foundational agricultural crops (corn, potatoes, tomatoes) and place names to governance concepts (influencing early American democracy) and ecological knowledge.
    • Affirming Sovereignty: Recognizing Indigenous peoples inherently acknowledges their inherent sovereignty as distinct nations with pre-existing rights to their lands and self-governance.

  3. Promotes Healing, Reconciliation, and Justice:

    • Validating Indigenous Experience: For Indigenous communities, the holiday is a powerful symbolic act of validation. It acknowledges their historical trauma and ongoing struggles, moving towards a more honest reckoning with the past.
    • Fostering Respect and Understanding: It challenges stereotypes, combats racism and prejudice, and encourages non-Indigenous people to learn about the true history and contemporary realities of Indigenous nations. This fosters greater empathy and respect.
    • Building Foundations for Reconciliation: Truth-telling is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation. Replacing a symbol of oppression with one of recognition and respect is a concrete step towards addressing historical wrongs and building more equitable relationships based on honesty and mutual respect.
    • Supporting Contemporary Struggles: Increased awareness and respect generated by the holiday can translate into greater support for Indigenous-led movements addressing critical issues like land back, water rights, treaty rights, missing and murdered Indigenous women (MMIW), and cultural preservation.

  4. Enriches National Identity and Education:

    • A More Accurate and Inclusive History: Adopting Indigenous Peoples' Day encourages a more complete and truthful national narrative. It moves beyond the myth of "discovery" to embrace the complex, multifaceted history of the land now called the United States.
    • Educational Opportunities: The holiday provides a meaningful context for schools and communities to teach accurate history about Indigenous peoples – their pre-contact societies, the realities of colonization, and their contemporary lives – fostering a more informed citizenry.
    • A Stronger, More Honest National Identity: Building a national identity on truth and inclusion, rather than myth and the erasure of others, creates a stronger, more just, and ultimately more authentic foundation for the country.

Conclusion:

Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day is not merely a change of name; it's a fundamental shift in perspective. It rejects the glorification of a figure synonymous with the violent onset of colonization and the attempted erasure of Indigenous peoples. Instead, it embraces truth-telling, honors the resilience and contributions of the original inhabitants of the Americas, and acknowledges the painful legacy that continues to impact Indigenous communities. The supposed benefits – fostering healing, promoting accurate history, celebrating vibrant cultures, building respect, and taking a step towards reconciliation – represent a significant step towards a more just, inclusive, and honest society for all its inhabitants, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous. It moves the focus from a celebration of conquest to one of recognition, respect, and the ongoing presence and contributions of Indigenous nations.

Rethinking Federal Holidays: The Case for Replacing Columbus Day

Introduction

Federal holidays represent our collective values and the figures we choose to honor as a nation. As our understanding of history deepens and becomes more inclusive, we face an important question: does Christopher Columbus merit a federal holiday? A growing number of historians, Indigenous groups, and communities argue that Columbus Day should be replaced with a holiday that better reflects American values and acknowledges historical truths.

The Historical Record

The traditional narrative of Columbus as a heroic explorer obscures documented historical facts:

Treatment of Indigenous Peoples: Primary sources, including Columbus's own journals and accounts from contemporaries like Bartolomé de las Casas, document brutal treatment of the Taíno people. Columbus enslaved Indigenous populations, implemented systems of forced labor, and oversaw violent punishments for those who failed to meet gold quotas.

Demographic Catastrophe: Whether through violence, forced labor, or introduced diseases, the Indigenous population of Hispaniola declined from hundreds of thousands to near extinction within decades of Columbus's arrival—a pattern repeated throughout colonized territories.

Personal Motivations: Columbus's voyages, while historically significant, were primarily motivated by personal wealth and glory rather than discovery or cultural exchange.

The Perspective of Indigenous Communities

For many Native Americans and Indigenous peoples throughout the Americas, Columbus Day represents celebration of their ancestors' oppression. Numerous tribal organizations have formally opposed the holiday, describing it as painful and disrespectful to their heritage.

Alternatives and Solutions

Rather than erasing this history, many propose replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day—a holiday already adopted by numerous states and municipalities. This alternative:

  • Acknowledges historical truth while promoting healing
  • Celebrates Indigenous cultures, contributions, and resilience
  • Educates future generations about complete American history
  • Maintains a federal holiday while shifting its meaning

Conclusion

Replacing Columbus Day doesn't mean erasing history—it means telling a more complete and honest version of it. As we evolve in our understanding, our symbols and celebrations should reflect our commitment to truth, justice, and inclusion.

Introduction

Every October, the United States faces a moral contradiction. Continuing to celebrate him with a federal holiday perpetuates historical myths and dishonors both the victims of colonialism and our nation's stated values of justice and human dignity.

The Myth Versus Historical Reality

The romanticized narrative of Columbus as a brave explorer who "discovered" America crumbles under historical scrutiny. Primary sources, including Columbus's own journals and contemporary accounts from Bartolomé de las Casas, reveal a conquistador who initiated systematic exploitation from his first voyage. Upon encountering the Arawak people, Columbus wrote, "They ought to make good and skilled servants, for they repeat very quickly whatever we say to them." This was not the observation of a benign explorer but the calculation of an enslaver.

The lands Columbus "discovered" were already home to millions of people with rich, complex civilizations. The Taíno people alone numbered between one and three million across the Caribbean islands. They had sophisticated agricultural systems, extensive trade networks, and vibrant cultures that had flourished for centuries. To celebrate Columbus's "discovery" is to perpetuate the racist notion that these lands and peoples only gained significance through European contact.

Documented Atrocities and Genocide

The historical record of Columbus's governance in the Americas reveals brutality that shocked even his contemporaries. As governor of Hispaniola, Columbus instituted a system of forced labor and tribute that decimated the Indigenous population. Every Taíno over fourteen was required to deliver a quota of gold dust or cotton every three months; those who failed had their hands severed—a punishment Columbus's men carried out with such frequency that it became systematic policy.

Under Columbus's rule, the Indigenous population of Hispaniola plummeted from an estimated 300,000 to 500,000 in 1492 to merely 500 by 1548. This catastrophic decline resulted from murder, suicide to escape enslavement, disease, and the complete disruption of Indigenous society. Spanish colonist and priest Bartolomé de las Casas documented how Columbus's men would test the sharpness of their blades by decapitating Indigenous people, hunt them with dogs for sport, and commit acts of sexual violence against women and children.

Columbus personally profited from selling Indigenous people into slavery, including children as young as nine years old. In a letter to Doña Juana de Torres, Columbus wrote about the slave trade with disturbing casualness: "A hundred castellanos are as easily obtained for a woman as for a farm, and there are plenty of dealers who go about looking for girls; those from nine to ten are now in demand."

The Foundation of Systemic Oppression

Columbus's voyages did not merely result in isolated acts of violence; they established templates for centuries of colonial exploitation. His encomienda system, which granted Spanish colonists the right to force Indigenous peoples into labor, became the blueprint for colonial labor systems throughout the Americas. This system directly enabled the extraction of vast wealth from the Americas while destroying Indigenous societies and economies.

Moreover, Columbus's expeditions initiated the transatlantic slave trade in the Americas. When Indigenous populations proved insufficient for colonial labor demands—largely because European diseases and violence had killed so many—colonizers turned to enslaving Africans. Columbus himself proposed and participated in this transition, forever linking his legacy to one of humanity's greatest crimes.

The colonization Columbus began resulted in the largest demographic catastrophe in human history. Scholars estimate that 90% of the Indigenous population of the Americas—between 50 to 100 million people—died within a century of European contact. While disease played a significant role, it spread through the deliberate destruction of Indigenous social structures, forced relocations, and the systematic impoverishment that Columbus pioneered.

Contemporary Harm and Cultural Impact

Maintaining Columbus Day as a federal holiday inflicts ongoing harm on Indigenous communities and distorts American historical consciousness. For Native Americans, the holiday represents a annual, government-sanctioned celebration of their ancestors' destruction. It trivializes genocide and sends a message that Indigenous lives and histories matter less than maintaining comfortable myths.

The holiday also perpetuates damaging stereotypes and historical inaccuracies in education. School children learn sanitized versions of Columbus's story that emphasize his "courage" and "discovery" while omitting or minimizing the violence he perpetrated. This miseducation contributes to broader ignorance about Indigenous peoples' histories and contemporary struggles. When we teach children to celebrate Columbus, we implicitly teach them that colonialism and its attendant violence are acceptable prices for "progress" and "civilization."

Furthermore, Columbus Day reinforces a Eurocentric narrative of American history that marginalizes not only Indigenous peoples but all communities of color. It suggests that American history began with European arrival, erasing millennia of Indigenous civilization and contributing to the systemic devaluation of non-European contributions to American society.

Defenders of Columbus Day often argue that we should not judge historical figures by contemporary moral standards. This argument fails on multiple levels. Celebrating these figures would honor Italian-American heritage without glorifying colonialism.

Some argue that abolishing Columbus Day would amount to "erasing history." On the contrary, it would mean teaching history more accurately and completely. No one suggests removing Columbus from history books or museums; the goal is to stop officially celebrating him with a federal holiday. We can acknowledge Columbus's historical significance while recognizing that significance is not synonymous with heroism.

A Path Forward: Indigenous Peoples' Day

Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples' Day offers an opportunity for historical reconciliation and education. This alternative holiday, already adopted by numerous states and municipalities, honors the resilience, contributions, and cultures of Native peoples while acknowledging the historical injustices they have endured.

Indigenous Peoples' Day provides a framework for teaching more complete and accurate history. It creates space for Americans to learn about the sophisticated societies that existed before European contact, the devastating impact of colonization, and the ongoing struggles and achievements of Native peoples. This education is not about guilt or blame but about understanding how historical injustices shape contemporary inequalities and how we might work toward reconciliation.

Ending the federal celebration of a figure who initiated these injustices while honoring those who survived them represents a meaningful, if symbolic, step toward this redress.

Conclusion

The abolition of Columbus Day as a federal holiday is not about political correctness or historical revisionism—it is about moral clarity and factual accuracy. Columbus's legacy is one of exploitation, enslavement, and genocide. His actions led directly to the deaths of millions and established systems of oppression that persist today. No amount of romanticization can change these facts.

As a nation, we have the power to choose whom we honor. We can continue to celebrate a man whose first thoughts upon meeting Indigenous peoples were how to enslave them, or we can choose to honor the Indigenous peoples who survived colonization and continue to enrich our nation. We can perpetuate myths that comfort some while causing pain to others, or we can embrace difficult truths that lead to greater understanding and reconciliation.

Abolishing Columbus Day does not mean forgetting history; it means remembering it fully and honestly. It means recognizing that America's story did not begin in 1492 but stretches back thousands of years through Indigenous civilizations. It means acknowledging that our nation's prosperity was built partly on profound injustices that we must reckon with to move forward.

The United States should immediately pass legislation to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with Indigenous Peoples' Day. This change would signal our commitment to truth over myth, justice over convenience, and reconciliation over continued harm. In doing so, we would take a crucial step toward becoming the nation we claim to be—one that truly values liberty, justice, and human dignity for all people.

Columbus’s legacy is inextricably tied to the colonization of the Americas, which laid the groundwork for centuries of Indigenous displacement, cultural erasure, and systemic oppression. Beyond the Myth: Why Abolishing Columbus Day Is a Moral Imperative for America

For over a century, the second Monday in October has been enshrined on the American calendar as Columbus Day—a federal holiday commemorating Christopher Columbus’s 1492 arrival in the Americas. Taught to generations through sanitized rhymes and heroic portraits, this observance presents a foundational myth of American identity: the brave explorer discovering a “New World.” Yet this narrative is not merely incomplete; it is a deliberate erasure of profound historical violence. Christopher Columbus’s legacy is inextricably bound to colonialism, systematic exploitation, and the catastrophic devastation of Indigenous peoples. To continue honoring him with a federal holiday is to endorse a sanitized history that inflicts ongoing harm on Native communities, perpetuates national myth-making, and obstructs the path toward genuine reconciliation. Abolishing Columbus Day is not an act of historical revisionism—it is an urgent moral correction, a necessary step toward truth, justice, and the honoring of Indigenous resilience.

The historical record of Columbus’s actions, meticulously documented by contemporaries and modern scholarship alike, reveals a legacy defined by brutality, not bravery. Upon landing in the Caribbean, Columbus initiated a regime of terror against the Taíno people of Guanahani (which he renamed San Salvador). His own ship logs betray his motives: he noted the Taíno’s generosity only to declare them “fit to be ruled” and “easily subjugated,” viewing them as commodities to be traded for gold. Within months, he instituted the encomienda system—a brutal framework of forced labor that enslaved Indigenous people in gold mines and plantations. Those who failed to meet quotas had their hands severed; dissenters were burned alive or fed to dogs. Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish priest who witnessed the atrocities firsthand, chronicled in A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies how Columbus’s men “attacked the Indians, stabbing them and cutting off their hands” and committed “unheard-of cruelty.” Under Columbus’s governorship, the Taíno population plummeted from an estimated 250,000–1 million to near extinction within 50 years due to massacre, starvation, disease exacerbated by forced displacement, and suicide. Historian Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz, in An Indigenous Peoples’ History of the United States, emphasizes that Columbus did not merely “discover” land—he launched the transatlantic slave trade (shipping 500 Taíno to Spain in 1495) and established the ideological blueprint for centuries of colonial genocide. To celebrate this man is to celebrate the architect of a system designed to erase entire civilizations.

Compounding this historical violence is the holiday’s own problematic genesis and enduring symbolism. Columbus Day was not established to honor Indigenous peoples or even primarily to celebrate exploration. Lobbied aggressively by the Knights of Columbus in the early 20th century, it was signed into federal law in 1937 largely as a gesture to counter anti-Italian and anti-Catholic bigotry—a worthy goal in itself. Yet in doing so, the holiday co-opted a figure whose actions directly enabled the Doctrine of Discovery, a 15th-century theological framework that declared non-Christian lands “empty” and ripe for seizure. This doctrine was later cited in the 1823 U.S. Supreme Court case Johnson v. M’Intosh to deny Indigenous land rights, cementing legal precedents that dispossessed Native nations for centuries. Federal recognition of Columbus Day since the Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 has thus functioned as state-sanctioned endorsement of this ideology. Every year the holiday is observed, it reinforces a national narrative that frames invasion as discovery, genocide as progress, and Indigenous erasure as inevitable. For Native children learning that the man who enslaved their ancestors is honored with a day off school, the message is clear: their history, their trauma, and their very existence are secondary to a myth of European triumph.

The continued federal observance of Columbus Day inflicts tangible harm. For Indigenous communities, it is a recurring trauma—a state-sponsored celebration of the violence that initiated centuries of forced removal, cultural suppression, and intergenerational suffering. As Dr. Debbie Reese (Nambé Owingeh), founder of American Indians in Children’s Literature, notes, such symbolism “teaches Native children that their ancestors’ pain is a footnote to someone else’s glory.” Beyond psychological injury, the holiday perpetuates educational malpractice. Textbooks and classroom activities often reduce Columbus to a “brave sailor,” omitting his role in initiating slavery and ecological devastation. This whitewashing impedes critical historical literacy and shields students from understanding the roots of contemporary inequities—from land dispossession to health disparities facing Native communities today. Meanwhile, the nation’s conscience remains fractured. How can the United States sincerely uphold values of equality and justice while federally venerating a man whose policies were condemned even by his contemporaries? Queen Isabella of Spain removed Columbus from his post as governor in 1500 due to his “cruelty and tyranny,” and de las Casas spent decades campaigning against the horrors Columbus unleashed. A nation that has rightly removed Confederate monuments and established Juneteenth as a federal holiday recognizing emancipation cannot logically sustain a holiday honoring colonial subjugation.

Skeptics often raise counterarguments, but each collapses under scrutiny. “Columbus was a product of his time” ignores that moral courage existed then as now. De las Casas, Indigenous resistors like Hatuey (who was burned at the stake warning others of Spanish cruelty), and even Spanish officials who investigated Columbus’s abuses prove that alternatives to brutality were recognized. Judging historical figures by evolving ethical standards is not anachronistic—it is the essence of moral progress. “He discovered America” is factually bankrupt: Indigenous peoples had thrived on these continents for millennia; Norse explorers reached North America centuries earlier; and Columbus never set foot on the continental United States. The word “discovery” itself is a colonial construct that renders Native peoples invisible. “Abolishing the holiday erases Italian-American heritage” is a false equivalence. Italian-American contributions to U.S. culture—from labor movements to arts—are profound and deserve celebration, but not through a figure whose legacy is antithetical to justice. Many Italian-American organizations, including Italian Americans for Indigenous Peoples’ Day, actively support replacement, advocating instead for honoring figures like labor activist Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini or celebrating heritage during October’s existing Italian-American Heritage Month. Finally, “It’s just a day off” dismisses the profound power of national symbols. Holidays teach us what a society values. We do not grant federal holidays to figures whose primary legacy is mass suffering—and we should not start with Columbus.

The path forward is clear, compassionate, and already gaining momentum. Since Berkeley, California, first replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day in 1992, over 15 states—including Maine, Vermont, New Mexico, and Alaska—and more than 130 cities have followed suit. South Dakota has observed Native Americans’ Day since 1990. These shifts honor living Indigenous cultures, celebrate resilience, and center truth: acknowledging historical trauma while uplifting contemporary Native voices, artists, and leaders. Indigenous Peoples’ Day transforms October from a celebration of conquest into an opportunity for education, reflection, and solidarity. Federally adopting this change would align national policy with the 2009 Native American Apology Resolution, which expressed regret for “the many instances of violence, maltreatment, and neglect” inflicted upon Native peoples. It would also follow the precedent of Juneteenth’s federal recognition—a powerful demonstration that America can correct its calendar to reflect hard-won truths. This is not about erasing history; it is about expanding it. Museums, classrooms, and historical sites can—and should—teach Columbus’s complex role with nuance. But a federal holiday is reserved for figures who embody our highest ideals. Columbus does not.

Abolishing Columbus Day is more than symbolic; it is a tangible act of restorative justice. It signals to Indigenous youth that their stories matter. It challenges all Americans to confront uncomfortable truths with courage rather than cling to comforting fictions. It affirms that a nation’s greatness lies not in denying its past, but in having the integrity to learn from it. As the late Cherokee scholar Dr. Vine Deloria Jr. urged, “We must stop pretending that history is a tidy story of heroes and villains.” Let us replace the myth of Columbus with the enduring truth of Indigenous survival. Let us replace a holiday rooted in conquest with one rooted in respect. In doing so, we do not diminish America—we deepen its commitment to the ideals of dignity, equality, and justice for all. The compass of history points toward reconciliation. It is time for our calendar to follow.

Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day: Rationale, Harms of the Original Holiday, and Benefits of the Shift

The movement to replace Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day (or regionally specific observances like Native American Day) reflects a decades-long effort—led primarily by Indigenous activists, educators, and allied communities—to reframe public commemoration toward historical accuracy, cultural respect, and social healing. First formally adopted by Berkeley, California, in 1992 (the 500th anniversary of Columbus’s 1492 voyage), this shift has since been embraced by over 15 U.S. states, hundreds of municipalities, universities, and institutions globally. Below is a balanced analysis grounded in historical evidence, Indigenous scholarship, and documented advocacy perspectives. Language prioritizes specificity (e.g., naming the Taíno people rather than generic terms) and centers Indigenous agency where possible.

I. Documented Harms of Celebrating Columbus Day

Critics—including historians, Indigenous nations, and human rights organizations—argue that venerating Columbus perpetuates tangible harms. These concerns are not merely about "judging history by modern standards" but about the ongoing consequences of glorifying a figure directly tied to documented atrocities and colonial frameworks.

  1. Historical Inaccuracy and Erasure

    • Columbus did not "discover" an empty land. The Americas were home to an estimated 50–100 million people across thousands of distinct, sovereign nations (e.g., the Taíno of the Caribbean, Haudenosaunee Confederacy, Diné, Maya) with advanced agricultural, scientific, and governance systems.
    • Celebrating Columbus reinforces the colonial myth of terra nullius ("empty land"), erasing millennia of Indigenous presence and innovation. It also overlooks earlier transoceanic contacts (e.g., Norse voyages) while centering a Eurocentric narrative that frames Indigenous peoples as passive recipients of "civilization."

  2. Documented Atrocities Linked to Columbus
    Primary sources—not modern reinterpretation—detail systematic violence under Columbus’s governorship of Hispaniola (1493–1500):

    • His journals describe enslaving Taíno people, imposing brutal gold quotas (with amputation for noncompliance), and trafficking Indigenous captives to Europe—actions condemned even by some contemporaries like Spanish priest Bartolomé de las Casas (A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies).
    • Policies initiated under Columbus accelerated catastrophic population collapse: forced labor, violence, and despair contributed to the near-eradication of the Taíno within decades. While disease played a role, historians like Andrés Reséndez (The Other Slavery) emphasize that Columbus’s actions catalyzed systems of exploitation that spread across the hemisphere. Many scholars (including the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) characterize this demographic collapse as genocide or ethnocide—a term reflecting intent to destroy a group’s existence.
    • Columbus’s voyages directly enabled the transatlantic slave trade’s expansion and established colonial frameworks (e.g., the encomienda system) that normalized Indigenous dispossession.

  3. Symbolic Violence and Intergenerational Trauma

    • For many Indigenous communities, Columbus Day is a painful reminder of invasion, broken treaties, forced assimilation (e.g., residential schools), and ongoing inequities (e.g., disproportionate rates of poverty, missing and murdered Indigenous women, land dispossession).
    • Glorifying Columbus validates colonial narratives that frame conquest as "progress," reinforcing stereotypes (e.g., the "vanishing Indian") and marginalizing Indigenous voices in public discourse. As the National Congress of American Indians states, such symbolism "perpetuates historical trauma and undermines healing."

  4. Educational Deficits
    Framing Columbus as a heroic explorer obscures critical historical complexity: Indigenous resistance (e.g., the 1680 Pueblo Revolt), pre-Columbian innovations (e.g., the Three Sisters agricultural system, Haudenosaunee governance influencing U.S. democracy), and the agency of Indigenous peoples. This incomplete history impedes reconciliation and fosters public misunderstanding.

II. Reasons and Documented Benefits of Honoring Indigenous Peoples

Replacing Columbus Day is not about "erasing history" but expanding commemoration to honor truth, resilience, and contemporary relevance. Proponents—including the International Indian Treaty Council, United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, and numerous tribal nations—highlight these evidence-based benefits:

A. For Indigenous Communities

  • Validation and Healing: Official recognition counters centuries of erasure. Events celebrating language revitalization (e.g., Cherokee Nation’s language programs), art, and ceremonies foster cultural pride, particularly for youth. Studies (e.g., American Journal of Public Health, 2020) link cultural connection to improved mental health outcomes in Indigenous youth.
  • Amplifying Contemporary Voices: The day spotlights modern Indigenous leadership—in climate justice (e.g., Diné resistance to fossil fuel extraction), law (e.g., Deb Haaland as first Indigenous U.S. Cabinet secretary), and arts (e.g., Joy Harjo as U.S. Poet Laureate)—challenging the myth that Indigenous peoples exist only in the past.
  • Supporting Sovereignty: Paired with concrete actions (land acknowledgments, repatriation of remains under NAGPRA), the holiday reinforces tribal sovereignty and aligns with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP).

B. For Education and Public Understanding

  • Curriculum Enrichment: Schools using the day to teach accurate history report deeper student engagement. Resources from organizations like IllumiNative and the National Museum of the American Indian help educators:
    • Highlight specific nations (avoiding pan-Indigenous generalizations).
    • Integrate Indigenous knowledge (e.g., fire stewardship practices now adopted by U.S. Forest Service).
    • Address contemporary issues (e.g., MMIW crisis, water protectors at Standing Rock).
  • Critical Thinking: Students learn to analyze multiple perspectives—e.g., comparing Columbus’s journals with Taíno oral histories—fostering media literacy and ethical reasoning. States like Maine report increased student interest in civic engagement after adopting Indigenous Peoples’ Day.

C. For Broader Society

  • Reconciliation and Solidarity: Symbolic change opens dialogue. Italian-American groups like the Italian American Heritage Foundation endorse the shift, noting Columbus (a Genoese sailing for Spain) does not represent Italian immigrant struggles. They advocate celebrating Italian heritage in October without conflating it with colonial violence—a model of cross-cultural solidarity.
  • Policy Momentum: Heightened visibility correlates with tangible progress:
    • Increased public support for legislation addressing Indigenous disparities (e.g., Savanna’s Act on MMIW).
    • Corporate partnerships funding Indigenous-led initiatives (e.g., Patagonia’s support for land-back movements).
  • Global Alignment: Similar shifts exist worldwide: Venezuela’s Día de la Resistencia Indígena, Argentina’s Día del Respeto a la Diversidad Cultural, and Canada’s National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. This reflects a hemispheric reckoning with colonialism endorsed by the Organization of American States.

Nuance and Common Misconceptions

  • "Erasing Italian-American Heritage?": Most advocates clarify the goal is not to diminish Italian contributions (celebrated widely during Italian American Heritage Month) but to decouple heritage from a figure whose documented actions caused profound harm. Many Italian-American organizations actively support Indigenous Peoples’ Day as an act of solidarity.
  • "Judging History Unfairly?": Historians note Columbus’s brutality was criticized in his own time (e.g., Spanish Crown recalled him for mismanagement). The critique targets the celebration of violence—not historical study. Teaching Columbus with nuance (including Indigenous perspectives) remains essential; the holiday shift simply redirects commemoration.
  • Indigenous Diversity: No single Indigenous perspective exists. While major organizations (e.g., National Congress of American Indians) strongly support the change, some communities prioritize other advocacy goals. The movement centers tribal sovereignty—honoring how each nation chooses to engage.
  • Symbolism vs. Substance: Advocates universally stress that holidays alone cannot rectify injustice. Indigenous Peoples’ Day is most impactful when paired with concrete actions: funding tribal education, honoring treaties, or supporting land-back initiatives. As scholar Dr. Debbie Reese (Nambé Owingeh) states: "This is about adding truth, not subtracting history."

Conclusion: Toward Inclusive Commemoration

Replacing Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day is a deliberate step toward historical honesty and relational repair. It rejects the glorification of colonial violence while uplifting the resilience, wisdom, and ongoing contributions of Indigenous peoples—who have stewarded these lands for millennia. The benefits extend beyond symbolism: enriched education, strengthened cultural identity, cross-community solidarity, and momentum for equitable policies.

This shift embodies a broader global movement—echoed in museum repatriations, truth commissions, and UNDRIP implementation—to ensure public memory reflects all who shape our world. As Indigenous leader Winona LaDuke (Ojibwe) articulates: "We are not asking to be remembered only in the past. We are asking to be seen, respected, and partnered with today." By centering Indigenous voices, societies move closer to commemorations that honor truth, foster healing, and build a more just future for everyone.

  • Explore resources: IllumiNative’s education toolkit; National Museum of the American Indian’s "Americans" exhibit.
  • Support Indigenous-led initiatives: Honor Native Land project; local tribal cultural centers.

The Case for Abolishing Columbus Day: Reckoning with a Legacy of Colonialism and Genocide

Introduction

Each year, federal buildings display Italian-American flags and schools hold celebrations as the nation observes Columbus Day. However, this commemoration of Christopher Columbus fails to acknowledge the darker realities of his legacy—one rooted in colonialism, genocide, and the systematic exploitation of Indigenous peoples. Rather than honoring a figure who initiated centuries of oppression, our nation should abolish this federal holiday and replace it with a celebration that reflects our values of justice, inclusivity, and respect for all communities.

Columbus's Role in Colonial Exploitation

Christopher Columbus's arrival in the Americas in 1492 marked the beginning of centuries of European colonization that would devastate Indigenous civilizations. Far from being a brave explorer discovering new worlds, Columbus served as an agent of Spanish colonial expansion with explicit mandates to extract wealth and enforce Spanish dominance.

Upon landing in the Caribbean, Columbus immediately established brutal encomiendas—systems of forced labor that treated Indigenous peoples as virtual slaves. He wrote in his journal about taking Indigenous people captive to be sold as slaves, noting that "I could capture hundreds of them and they would not resist." This exploitation became systematic under his governance as viceroy, where he implemented gold tribute systems that demanded exorbitant portions of Indigenous labor and resources.

Columbus also introduced European diseases to which Indigenous populations had no immunity. Smallpox, measles, and other pathogens decimated native populations, contributing significantly to the demographic collapse that saw millions of Indigenous people perish within decades of contact.

Genocide and Systematic Violence Against Indigenous Peoples

The historical record documents Columbus's direct involvement in acts that constitute genocide. After the Taíno people resisted Spanish rule, Columbus ordered punitive expeditions that resulted in mass killings, mutilation, and enslavement. Spanish chroniclers recorded how Columbus's men would attack Indigenous villages, killing men and taking women and children as prisoners.

Archaeological and historical evidence shows that Columbus established the first concentration camps in the Americas at Nahuatl Ruins and other locations, where Indigenous people were held in captivity before being shipped to Spain. The population decline of the Taíno people—from an estimated 1 million to fewer than 500 survivors within 50 years—represents one of the first genocides of the Americas, directly traceable to Spanish colonization initiated by Columbus.

The Myth of "Discovery" and Its Harmful Implications

The very premise of Columbus Day perpetuates the myth that Columbus "discovered" the Americas, erasing the sophisticated civilizations that already existed. Thousands of years of Indigenous culture, governance, and astronomical knowledge were rendered invisible by this narrative. This revisionist history serves to justify subsequent displacement and marginalization of Native peoples while ignoring their ongoing presence and contributions to American society.

Furthermore, the holiday sends a harmful message to Indigenous communities and all citizens about whose lives and histories matter. Celebrating Columbus while ignoring the devastating impact of his actions reflects a national failure to confront uncomfortable truths about our founding and expansion.

Economic Exploitation and Encomienda System

Columbus's economic policies were designed purely for extraction of wealth rather than sustainable development or mutual benefit. He established the encomienda system, which granted Spanish settlers rights to Indigenous labor without compensation. This system legalized forced labor and debt peonage, creating conditions akin to slavery that persisted throughout the colonial period.

His policies also included brutal reprisals against Indigenous communities that failed to meet gold production quotas. Spanish records document how Columbus ordered the execution of Indigenous leaders who couldn't produce sufficient tribute, demonstrating the violent methods used to maintain economic exploitation.

Abolishing Columbus Day would allow America to move toward a more honest reckoning with its past. Several cities and states have already replaced the holiday with Indigenous Peoples' Day, recognizing the original inhabitants of this land and their ongoing contributions to American society.

This change would send an important message about our nation's commitment to truth and reconciliation. It would acknowledge that celebrating colonial conquest does not align with democratic values of equality and human dignity. Instead, we could honor the resilience and rich cultures of Indigenous peoples while learning from their experiences and perspectives.

Columbus Day, as currently celebrated, perpetuates historical myths that obscure the realities of colonization and its ongoing impacts on Indigenous communities. A federal holiday should inspire unity and shared values, yet honoring Columbus accomplishes neither when his legacy centers on exploitation, violence, and cultural destruction.

The United States has the opportunity to demonstrate leadership in addressing historical injustices by abolishing this federal holiday. In doing so, we can begin to heal divisions, honor the truth about our past, and build a more inclusive future that respects all communities. True patriotism requires the courage to confront uncomfortable truths rather than celebrating figures whose actions contradict our highest ideals of justice and human dignity.

Our national holidays should reflect who we aspire to become, not who we were forced to endure. It is time to replace Columbus Day with a celebration that honors the original peoples of this land and the values of truth, justice, and reconciliation that define a mature democracy.

A Legacy of Blood: Why Columbus Day Must Be Abolished

For over a century, the United States has set aside the second Monday of October to commemorate Christopher Columbus. Parades, school assemblies, and closed government offices reinforce the image of a heroic navigator who “discovered” a New World. Yet beneath the veneer of celebration lies a dark reality: Columbus’s legacy is not one of noble exploration, but of colonialism, genocide, and the systematic exploitation of Indigenous peoples. To continue honoring him with a federal holiday is to sanitize history, to inflict ongoing harm on Native communities, and to perpetuate a founding myth that has justified centuries of oppression. It is time to abolish Columbus Day as a federal holiday and replace it with a commemoration that acknowledges the true cost of European contact—and the resilience of those who survived it.

The historical record leaves no doubt that Columbus’s voyages unleashed devastation upon the Indigenous inhabitants of the Caribbean. When Columbus first sighted the Bahamas in 1492, he described the Taíno people as “gentle,” “free from covetousness,” and “suitable for every purpose.” Yet within days of making landfall, he ordered six of them seized and taken aboard his ships, writing in his journal: “I could conquer the whole of them with fifty men and govern them as I pleased.” This early impulse to dominate foreshadowed the brutality to come.

Appointed governor of the Indies, Columbus implemented policies that reduced the Taíno population from an estimated 300,000–1,000,000 in 1492 to just a few hundred by 1508. His men raped, enslaved, and murdered with impunity. They forced Indigenous people to labor in gold mines under the encomienda system, where starvation, overwork, and European diseases (to which the Taíno had no immunity) decimated communities. Columbus himself admitted to enslaving hundreds and sending them to Spain for sale. In a 1495 letter, he boasted of capturing 1,500 people in a single raid, remarking that “they will all be sold” to repay the Crown’s investment. Such actions were not aberrations; they were the engine of a colonial enterprise built on human suffering.

The consequences extended far beyond the Caribbean. Columbus’s voyages inaugurated a transatlantic slave trade that would eventually engulf millions of Africans, and his example emboldened other conquistadors to repeat the pattern of conquest across the Americas. To celebrate Columbus Day is to celebrate the beginning of a hemispheric catastrophe—a fact that modern historians like Howard Zinn and Bartolomé de las Casas (whose A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies documented the atrocities) have long recognized. Las Casas, a contemporary of Columbus, wrote in horror: “Such inhumanities and barbarisms were committed in my sight as no age can parallel.”

Defenders of the holiday often argue that it honors Italian-American heritage or the spirit of exploration. These arguments, while well-intentioned, fail to justify the federal endorsement of a figure whose actions would today be classified as crimes against humanity. Italian-Americans have a rich cultural history that deserves celebration—but that celebration need not be tethered to a man who symbolizes colonial violence. Indeed, many Italian-American organizations, including the National Italian American Foundation, have begun to distance themselves from Columbus, recognizing that their heritage encompasses far more than a 15th-century genocidaire. As for exploration, history offers countless examples of voyagers who expanded human knowledge without enslaving or exterminating the people they encountered. Celebrating Columbus confuses the act of sailing with the morality of the consequences.

Moreover, the federal holiday perpetuates a false narrative that erases Indigenous agency and presence. The myth of “discovery” implies that the Americas were empty prior to European arrival—a deliberate ignoring of the sophisticated civilizations that thrived for millennia. It also marginalizes the contemporary struggles of Native peoples, who must watch their tax dollars support a holiday that glorifies their ancestors’ dispossession. For many Indigenous communities, Columbus Day is a painful reminder of ongoing marginalization; it is experienced not as a celebration, but as a slap in the face. As the Lakota activist Bill Means stated, “Columbus Day represents the ideology of colonization—the same ideology that justified the taking of our lands, the breaking of treaties, and the silencing of our voices.”

The movement to replace Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day has gained momentum across the United States. Since 1990, more than a dozen states and over 130 cities have either abolished Columbus Day or renamed it. South Dakota celebrates Native American Day; Vermont and Maine have replaced it with Indigenous Peoples’ Day; even conservative states like Alaska have moved away from Columbus. These changes reflect a growing consensus: a federal holiday should unite Americans, not divide them by honoring a figure who represents the worst of our colonial past.

Critics argue that abolishing the holiday constitutes “erasing history.” Nothing could be further from the truth. Abolishing Columbus Day does not mean ignoring Columbus; it means refusing to grant him a pedestal. History should be studied in all its complexity, including the violence of colonization. But a federal holiday is not a neutral act of remembrance—it is an endorsement, a signal of national values. By continuing to honor Columbus, the United States implicitly tells its citizens that genocide and exploitation can be celebrated if they occurred long enough ago. That is a dangerous message.

The time has come for the federal government to catch up with the moral arc of the nation. Abolishing Columbus Day would be a small but significant step toward acknowledging historical injustices and fostering reconciliation. It would open space for a more honest reckoning with the past—one that recognizes the resilience and contributions of Indigenous peoples, who have survived and continue to thrive despite five centuries of systemic oppression.

In conclusion, Christopher Columbus’s legacy is one of blood and broken treaties, not discovery and progress. A federal holiday in his name is an affront to the millions who suffered under colonial rule and to the Indigenous communities who still bear the scars. We must retire Columbus Day, not to rewrite history, but to stop celebrating its darkest chapters. Let us replace it with Indigenous Peoples’ Day—a holiday that honors the original inhabitants of this land, acknowledges the truth of what happened here, and charts a more inclusive course for the future. Only then can we begin to heal the wounds of the past and build a nation that truly values all its people.

Part 1: Harms of Celebrating Columbus Day

The case for replacing Columbus Day rests on the documentable harms of centering Columbus as a heroic national figure, which extends far beyond individual historical critique to uphold damaging colonial narratives and ongoing systemic injustice.

1. Historical Inaccuracy and Erasure

The core myth of Columbus Day—that Columbus "discovered" the Americas—relies on deliberate erasure:

  • Indigenous peoples had lived in the Americas for at least 10,000 years prior to European contact, building complex, sovereign civilizations including the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy, the Mississippian mound-building cultures, the Ancestral Puebloans, and the Taino of the Caribbean.   • The claim that Columbus proved the Earth was round is false: European, Indigenous, and Islamic scholars had accepted the Earth’s spherical shape for centuries before 1492.

2. Commemoration of Genocide and Colonial Violence

Columbus’s own journals, accounts from his crew, and Spanish colonial records confirm that his voyages launched a campaign of extreme violence against Indigenous peoples:

  • Upon reaching Hispaniola (modern-day Dominican Republic and Haiti), Columbus enslaved Taino people, forced them to mine gold under threat of mutilation (cutting off the hands of those who failed to meet quotas), and permitted Spanish colonists to seize Indigenous women and girls as sexual slaves.

Columbus’s voyages were justified by the 15th-century Doctrine of Discovery, a series of papal bulls that granted European Christian nations the legal right to seize land inhabited by non-Christians. Celebrating Columbus reinforces this colonial legal framework, which continues to block Indigenous communities from reclaiming stolen land and exercising self-governance today.

Generations of U.S. students learn a sanitized, heroic narrative of Columbus as a brave explorer, rather than the full history of colonization. The shift to Indigenous Peoples’ Day is not intended to erase Italian American heritage (many municipalities now observe Italian Heritage Day alongside the new holiday to honor both histories), but to correct harmful narratives and affirm the value of Indigenous peoples and cultures. 1. Accurate, Inclusive Historical Representation

Indigenous Peoples’ Day replaces the "discovery" myth with a fact-based account of pre-contact Indigenous civilizations, the violence of colonization, and the ongoing existence of Indigenous nations. It reorients public memory to recognize that "discovery" is a colonial term that denies Indigenous people’s inherent ownership of their land, and that the U.S. was founded on land stolen from sovereign Indigenous nations. 2. Reparative Recognition of Indigenous Sovereignty and Resilience

The holiday explicitly acknowledges that Indigenous peoples are not a historical footnote, but living, sovereign nations with distinct cultures, governments, and rights, as affirmed by the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), which the U.S. endorsed in 2010. It is a small but meaningful step toward reparative justice, centering Indigenous voices in public discourse and validating the survival of Indigenous communities after centuries of colonization.

3. Cultural Visibility and Preservation

Indigenous Peoples’ Day celebrations are typically Indigenous-led, featuring powwows, storytelling, language revitalization workshops, art exhibitions, and public education events that center Indigenous culture. This counteracts decades of forced assimilation and cultural erasure, supports Indigenous communities in preserving their heritage, and fosters pride among Indigenous youth, who are disproportionately likely to face erasure in mainstream curriculum and media.

The holiday pushes K-12 and public education systems to integrate Indigenous perspectives, histories, and contributions: for example, Indigenous agricultural innovations (corn, potatoes, tomatoes, and chili peppers, which transformed global diets), Indigenous governance systems (such as the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, which some scholars argue influenced early U.S. democratic frameworks), and histories of Indigenous resistance to colonization. 5. Spurring Policy Action on Indigenous Rights

Public recognition of Indigenous history and the harms of colonization builds momentum for policy changes to address long-standing injustices: this includes addressing the MMIWG crisis, fulfilling unkept treaty obligations, improving Indigenous healthcare and education, advancing land back initiatives, and protecting Indigenous sacred sites from extraction and development. The holiday also aligns U.S. domestic policy with international human rights frameworks, including UNDRIP.

Indigenous communities have developed thousands of years of traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) around sustainable land and water management, wildfire mitigation, and climate adaptation. For example, Indigenous cultural burning practices were suppressed by colonial fire suppression policies, contributing to the catastrophic wildfires that now plague the U.S. West; integrating TEK into modern policy has already proven effective at reducing fire risk and restoring ecosystems. Indigenous food sovereignty practices also address food insecurity and promote sustainable, healthy diets for all communities.

Replacing Columbus Day is not an act of historical erasure, but a correction of a long-standing, harmful myth. While the original holiday was intended to support Italian American communities facing discrimination, the shift to Indigenous Peoples’ Day honors that heritage while also affirming the rights, history, and humanity of Indigenous peoples. It is a step toward a more just, honest, and inclusive society that recognizes the full, complex history of the Americas.

The Unconquerable Horror: Why Columbus Day Must Be Abolished

Every second Monday of October, the United States federal government closes its doors, postal services halt, and many Americans enjoy a day of rest in honor of Christopher Columbus. Maintaining Columbus Day as a federal holiday is not only historically dishonest but morally indefensible. The United States must abolish Columbus Day and, in doing so, finally reject the celebration of conquest in favor of truth, accountability, and respect for Indigenous survival.

The foundational justification for Columbus Day rests upon a myth that collapses under even cursory historical scrutiny: the notion that Columbus “discovered” America. This narrative requires the erasure of millions of Indigenous peoples who had inhabited the Western Hemisphere for tens of thousands of years, developing sophisticated civilizations, complex agricultural systems, and extensive trade networks long before European ships darkened their shores. Moreover, Columbus himself never actually reached the landmass of the present-day United States; he stumbled upon islands in the Caribbean, believing until his death that he had arrived in Asia. He was, by his own admission, geographically lost. To venerate him as a discoverer is to endorse a pernicious colonial logic that renders Indigenous peoples invisible and defines history solely through the lens of European expansion. A federal holiday built upon such intellectual dishonesty does not educate the public—it indoctrinates them into accepting the supremacy of conquest over coexistence.

Far worse than the myth of discovery, however, is the brutal reality of what Columbus actually did upon making landfall. His journal entries and the accounts of those who accompanied him reveal a man driven by greed and religious fanaticism, who viewed the Indigenous Taino people not as human beings but as commodities to be exploited. Upon arriving in the Bahamas and later establishing a settlement on Hispaniola (present-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic), Columbus immediately initiated the transatlantic slave trade in Indigenous peoples, shipping hundreds of captives back to Spain to be sold. Those who remained were forced into a system of brutal labor to extract gold, meeting quotas under threat of mutilation or death. The Spanish priest Bartolomé de las Casas, an eyewitness to these atrocities, documented horrors that defy sanitization: mass suicides as Indigenous peoples fled the cruelty of Spanish rule, infants dying of starvation as their mothers were overworked, and the systematic dismemberment of those who failed to satisfy Spanish avarice. Within two generations of Columbus’s arrival, the Taino population of Hispaniola plummeted from an estimated hundreds of thousands—or perhaps millions—to mere remnants, annihilated by a combination of enslavement, mass murder, and introduced diseases that spread rapidly through populations traumatized by violence and displacement. This was not incidental to Columbus’s legacy; it was its inevitable consequence. To celebrate Columbus is to celebrate the inauguration of a genocide.

Defenders of the holiday sometimes argue that Columbus should be judged by the standards of his time, as if fifteenth-century Europe uniformly endorsed the enslavement and extermination of newly encountered peoples. This apologia fails on two counts. First, Columbus’s own contemporaries recognized his barbarity. During his third voyage, Spanish authorities arrested him and shipped him back to Europe in chains, appalled by reports of his tyrannical governance and the chaos of Hispaniola. If his cruelty was unremarkable for the era, his peers would not have found it necessary to imprison him. Second, the “standards of the time” argument is itself a historical sleight of hand that ignores Indigenous standards of the time—the laws, ethics, and human dignities that existed among the nations Columbus encountered and subsequently destroyed. Moral relativism cannot be deployed selectively to excuse atrocities while ignoring the voices of the victims. A federal holiday is not a neutral historical marker; it is an endorsement. By continuing to enshrine Columbus in the national calendar, the United States government implicitly validates the Doctrine of Discovery—the pseudo-legal framework that justified Indigenous dispossession—and signals that the lives extinguished by colonialism matter less than the reputations of those who extinguished them.

This argument, while acknowledging a genuine desire for ethnic pride, rests upon a false choice. Italian-Americans have given immeasurable contributions to American society—in science, labor organizing, art, politics, and civil rights. Their legacy deserves commemoration, but it need not be anchored to a figure whose primary historical significance is the unleashing of Indigenous suffering. Communities can and should honor Italian-American heritage through figures who embody democratic values and human dignity, rather than through a man who inaugurated centuries of colonial violence. To insist that Italian-American identity is inseparable from Columbus is to accept a narrative constructed not by Italian immigrants themselves, but by political elites in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries who used Columbus to assimilate Italian immigrants into a white American identity defined, in part, against Indigenous and Black peoples. Dismantling this association liberates Italian-American heritage from the baggage of colonialism rather than diminishing it.

Abolishing Columbus Day is not merely an act of negation; it is an essential step toward restorative justice and historical reckoning. A federal holiday recognizing Indigenous peoples would signal a commitment to addressing these ongoing injustices rather than mythologizing their origins.

The United States cannot credibly profess commitment to human rights, equality, and justice while continuing to devote a national holiday to a man whose legacy is written in Indigenous blood. Every year that Columbus Day persists, the government rehearses a lie that sanitizes genocide and normalizes the theft of Indigenous land. The abolition of this holiday is the bare minimum standard of moral coherence for a nation that aspires to democratic principles. It is time to remove Columbus from his undeserved pedestal and replace him with a truth that honors the Indigenous peoples who survived his brutality and continue to shape the Americas. In the annals of history, few figures evoke as much controversy as Christopher Columbus. Title: Reclaiming History: The Imperative to Abolish Columbus Day

Introduction
Every October, millions of Americans observe Columbus Day, a federal holiday celebrating the arrival of Christopher Columbus in 1492. Yet, beneath this patriotic veneer lies a grim reality: Columbus’s legacy is one of colonialism, genocide, and exploitation. To honor a figure responsible for the systemic destruction of Indigenous peoples is to perpetuate historical injustice. This essay argues that Columbus Day should be abolished, replaced by Indigenous Peoples’ Day, to acknowledge the truth and honor the resilience of Native communities.

Historical Context and Myths
Established in 1937 as Columbus Day and later enshrined as a federal holiday, the day reflects a Eurocentric narrative that glorifies exploration while erasing Indigenous suffering. Columbus’s voyages, touted as “discovery,” were inherently violent acts of colonization. His journals reveal unapologetic brutality, such as his 1492 order to burn Spanish villages and enslave inhabitants who refused tribute. The myth of a benign explorer obscures the reality: Columbus’s arrival triggered a catastrophic era for Native Americans.

Columbus’s Actions: Brutality and Exploitation
Columbus’s expedition was marked by systemic violence. During his second voyage (1493), he enslaved over 1,500 Taíno people, subjecting them to torture and forced labor. In 1496, he orchestrated the Massacre of Caloosahatchee, slaughtering hundreds of peaceful Calusa inhabitants. His reign of terror laid the groundwork for Spain’s colonial machinery, including the encomienda system, which legalized Indigenous enslavement. Columbus’s legacy is not exploration but exploitation, a precursor to the genocide that followed.

Impact on Indigenous Peoples
Columbus’s arrival catalyzed the demographic collapse of the Americas. Disease, introduced by Europeans, wiped out an estimated 90% of Indigenous populations within a century. Survivors faced cultural erasure, forced conversion, and displacement. The destruction was not merely physical but existential; languages, traditions, and autonomy were systematically dismantled. Indigenous resistance, such as the Taino uprising in Puerto Rico, underscores their enduring struggle against oppression.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals
Proponents of Columbus Day argue that he “opened” the New World, enabling cultural exchange. However, this “exchange” was one-sided: Indigenous peoples were decimated, while European colonization entrenched systemic racism. The economic “benefits” to Europe came at a genocidal cost. Recognizing Columbus as a hero ignores the voices of Indigenous scholars, such as Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz, who emphasize that colonization was a “project of conquest, not curiosity.”

Towards a Just Reckoning
Several states, including California and New York, have replaced Columbus Day with Indigenous Peoples’ Day, a move endorsed by the National Congress of American Indians. This renaming acknowledges Indigenous resilience and centers their perspectives. Federal recognition of such a day would send a powerful message: the U.S. values truth over myth. Educating students about Indigenous histories and sovereignty can further rectify historical erasure.

Conclusion
Abolishing Columbus Day is not an attack on history but a commitment to truth-telling. By honoring Indigenous resilience through Indigenous Peoples’ Day, we honor the victims of colonialism and reaffirm our moral obligation to justice. To celebrate Columbus is to perpetuate his atrocities; to honor Indigenous Peoples is to heal. The time has come to rewrite this chapter in American history—one rooted in empathy, accuracy, and respect.

References

  • Dunbar-Ortiz, R. (2014). An Indigenous Peoples’ History of the United States. Haymarket Books.
  • Zinn, H. (1980). A People’s History of the United States. Harper & Row.
  • National Congress of American Indians. (2023). Indigenous Peoples’ Day. https://ncai.org

This essay urges a radical shift in how we commemorate history, advocating not for the erasure of the past but for its honest reclamation.
